newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - French left leader bruised before battle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - French left leader bruised before battle.

text.p: When he stunned all, including himself, by losing the French presidency only narrowly in 1995, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin could do no wrong.
But almost two years after he polled 47.5 percent against Gaullist Jacques Chirac, the austere silver-haired challenger is floundering in the run-up to a general election due next March.
Two self-inflicted blows have bruised the popularity of the country's largest opposition force.
The far-right, anti-immigration National Front humiliated Jospin's party in February when it crushed a Socialist incumbent embroiled in legal trouble in the southern town of Vitrolles.

Days later, hundreds of artists and intellectuals launched nationwide protests against a government-sponsored bill to clamp down on illegal immigration. An embarrassed Socialist party was forced to jump on the bandwagon late.
"This has to be Jospin's worst phase since he lost the presidency," said Pascal Perrineau, politics professor at the Sciences Po institute.

"The confidence he had built shows signs of erosion in the polls. In the past month, the Socialist party has appeared hesitant, its pledges and its actions are out of step. That's a legacy of the late president Francois Mitterrand which Jospin had previously managed to erase," Perrineau said.
BUMBLING SIMPLETON IN TV SHOW
The popular Guignols de l'Info (news clowns) television show lampooned Jospin for months as "Yoyo in the land of ideas", a bumbling simpleton in a toy car searching for policies.
It now awards his professorial puppet a "statutory minute" to flannel on the issues while his lieutenants tear their hair out at his feebleness.
All too often, says the satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine, the real-life Jospin's speeches taste like bland, lukewarm tea.
The bespectacled Jospin, 59, is disarmingly candid about his image. "Politics has tended to freeze and starch the man that I am," he said in a typically stitlted television interview.
"Victory is not certain, but everything is still possible," was the closest he could come to a rallying cry in a recent speech to Socialist candidates at Paris's Science Park.
He urged them to pay attention to ordinary voters' concerns and embody resistance to the National Front.
The ruling centre-right coalition has increased its lead in the latest opinion polls after a period when the Socialists and their left-wing allies edged to within striking distance.
Resisting image spin-doctors eager to redesign him, Jospin has picked the specifics of the election manifesto as the focus for his lunge out of the doldrums.

The economic platform he unveiled in March proposed to shrink the working week to 35 hours without cutting pay, create 700,000 jobs, mostly for the young, in two years, and reform health insurance payments.

His telegenic backdrop was aimed at flagging his commitment to European Union -- blending the golden stars of the EU symbol and the French tricolor. But in deference to a public mood of Euro-scepticism, he has soft-pedalled EU issues.
An IPSOS opinion poll for France 2 television showed he has much convincing ahead. The economic platform failed to convince 46 percent of voters. Only 21 percent approved.
Fifty-five percent said it was little different from the government's policy, and a similar proportion dismissed the job-creation pledge as unrealistic.
ROUNDS ON JUPPE AS AUTHORITARIAN
Jospin has also sought to sound more combative, attacking Juppe as "authoritarian, brusque but inefficient".
The Socialist leader has accused the government of seeking to lure voters from Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right National Front by mimicking its anti-immigrant ideas.

"The main aim of Jospin's offensive from now is to shift the political debate away from immigration and the National Front. He knows he has a handicap there because he is not the master of the issues involved," Perrineau said.
He suggested Jospin's uncharismatic decency could yet turn out to be an asset at a time of public disenchantment with politicians' unkept promises and widespread sleaze.

"Jospin could try to change his image, but he showed in the presidential campaign that his weaknesses can turn to strengths. He may appear naive sometimes but that also makes him seem more genuine, more ethical than others," Perrineau added.
Jospin has managed to virtually stamp out the infighting which plagued the Socialists through the Mitterrand years, but left-wingers and young Turks are snapping at his heels.

His refusal to break with the single European currency, let alone with the market economy, is anathema to diehard leftists and the main stumbling-block in his attempt to forge an electoral pact with the Communists and the Greens.
Nor did his arm's length approach to the immigration row win him many plaudits.
"Politicians must match their words and their deeds...In the immigration debate, the Left did not defend its own values enough," said Socialist former labour minister Martine Aubry.
Jospin's longtime party rival, former prime minister Laurent Fabius, has outshone him with several hard-hitting speeches, full of the media-friendly soundbites that Jospin shuns.
In his determination to eschew demagogy, the Socialist leader sometimes sounds short on ambition.
"Given our starting point, we cannot meet with defeat," Jospin told his troops, referring to the party's tiny National Assembly presence of only 63 out of 577 seats following a 1993 landslide defeat.
"We will meet with success. Whether this success is a triumph depends a great deal on us," he said.
